name: The First Month — Parallel Operations
title: What Happened in the Weeks After the Princess Died, and Who Was Paying Attention
date: Highsun 1–30, 955 BF — The First Month of the Post-Assassination Period
location: Multiple — Mushroom Kingdom Capital / Sarasaland Emergency Bunker / Donut Plains Neutral Settlement / Bowser's Schoolhouse (Valley of Bowser Adjacent) / Kivotos Millennium Science School / Equestrian Diplomatic Circuit
type: Parallel Incident Compilation — Three Simultaneous Threads Running Concurrently with the Active Cover-Up
status: Partially Resolved — Daisy reached the bunker, the Kivotos concordant was negotiated, Baldi confirmed knowledge of the liquid and went silent; none of these threads reached conclusions because the first month never reached conclusions, it only reached the second month
note: Waluigi is compiling three separate incident threads here because they occurred during the same compressed window — the first thirty days after the assassination — and because their simultaneity is the point. While the Regency was eliminating witnesses, while Toadsmith was finding the journal, while the cover-up was being constructed in real time, the rest of the world was also moving. Sarasaland was evacuating its princess. A diplomat from Equestria was making the rounds of the Doughnut World's institutions with a concordant nobody had asked for. A schoolteacher in a building that has no business existing in this timeline recognized a vial of something terrible and went very quiet about it. None of these threads are connected by conspiracy. They are connected by proximity to a kingdom-sized wound that was bleeding into everything around it. When something this significant dies, the death does not stay inside its borders. It seeps. Waluigi has been tracking the seepage for a long time. WAH.
summary: In the thirty days following Princess Peach's assassination on Highsun 1, 955 BF, three parallel incidents unfolded across multiple locations simultaneously with the active construction of the Regency's cover-up. Princess Daisy of Sarasaland, receiving fragmentary and possibly inaccurate intelligence about her sister's death and Mario's disappearance, evacuated to a secure bunker via a pilot she correctly identified as a liability and incorrectly trusted anyway. While in the bunker, her tactical staff identified Fawful's forces as a possible third-party actor in the assassination, complicating the official Bowser-as-assassin narrative that the Regency was simultaneously constructing. A diplomat identified only as Agent T, operating on behalf of the Mushroom Regency, visited multiple institutions across the Doughnut World to negotiate suppression agreements and distribute an unusual liquid of unknown composition for analysis — visiting both Baldi's Schoolhouse and Millennium Science School in Kivotos, where they negotiated the Pony Halo Concordant with student council representative Hanaoka Yuzu. Baldi, upon analyzing the liquid, displayed recognition and then went silent in a manner that Waluigi considers significant. These three threads did not intersect. They did not coordinate. They were simply happening at the same time, in a world that did not yet know how long the cover-up would last.
description:
Waluigi needs to establish something before proceeding with the individual threads: the first thirty days after an assassination are not the beginning of the aftermath. They ARE the aftermath. Everything that happens in the first month is happening while the wound is still open, while the blood is still moving, while the people who caused the wound are still in the room. The Regency did not cover up a historical event. They covered up a current event, in real time, while the kingdom watched the balcony where Peach never appeared and tried to understand what it was seeing.

This is why the parallel threads matter. The Regency's cover-up was not operating in a vacuum. It was operating alongside a Sarasaland evacuation, a diplomatic circuit, a schoolteacher who recognized something he should not have recognized, and a student council representative who negotiated a concordant with an Equestrian agent while the kingdom burned. The world does not pause for cover-ups. The world continues, and the cover-up has to contend with a world that is continuing.

Waluigi finds this analytically significant because most historical analysis of the post-assassination period focuses on the Regency's actions. The Regency eliminated witnesses. The Regency controlled the investigation. The Regency constructed the narrative. This is all true. But it happened in a world that included Daisy evacuating to a bunker, Baldi going quiet, and Hanaoka Yuzu negotiating border policy over tea. The cover-up did not happen in a controlled environment. It happened in chaos. And chaos leaves gaps.

Waluigi has spent considerable time examining the gaps.

## Thread One:


The Sarasaland Evacuation — What Daisy Knew and When She Knew It

Princess Daisy of Sarasaland received her intelligence about the assassination in fragments, through channels that were already degraded by the time the news reached her. This is important. The information she acted on was incomplete, potentially corrupted, and arrived during a period when the Regency was actively managing what information left the capital. Daisy did not have access to the truth. She had access to what the Regency allowed to escape the capital, plus whatever her own intelligence networks could assemble from the chaos.

What she believed, based on available intelligence: Peach was dead. Bowser had been present. Luigi had fought Bowser and won — which Toadsworth correctly identified as anomalous, because Luigi winning against Bowser without Mario is not a standard outcome and the anomaly suggests the circumstances were non-standard. Mario was missing. The situation was active and dangerous.

What she did not know: that the Regency was constructing a narrative around Bowser's presence. That the Mages' Guild had already assumed investigative jurisdiction. That the guard witnesses were already dying. That the cover-up was already in motion and that her intelligence, fragmentary as it was, was already more accurate than what the official investigation would eventually produce.

Waluigi notes the specific exchange that Toadsworth initiated during the evacuation helicopter flight: 'my intel could still be bad. Mario could still be okay.' This is the correct analytical instinct applied to the wrong concern. Toadsworth was worrying about whether the death itself was real. The more important question — one that apparently nobody in Daisy's immediate circle was asking — was why the death had occurred and who had arranged for Bowser to be present when it did.

Bowser showing up at Peach's castle the night she died is not evidence that Bowser killed her. Bowser had a documented history of invading Peach's castle for other reasons. If someone had known in advance that Bowser would invade — if someone had, hypothetically, arranged for the conditions that made invasion likely — then Bowser's presence was not evidence of guilt. It was evidence that someone had arranged for him to be there as a convenient scapegoat.

Daisy's bunker analysis team reached this conclusion independently, which Waluigi considers significant. They identified Fawful as a possible third-party actor within the same first month that the Regency was constructing the Bowser-as-assassin narrative. Without access to the Mages' Guild's evidence. Without the chronicle. Without the journal. Simply by looking at the available intelligence and asking who else might have had both motive and capability.

Fawful. The mad tactician. A figure who had demonstrated sufficient intelligence and strategic capacity to cause major disruptions in the past, who had aligned himself with forces the conventional kingdom had not anticipated, and who — crucially — had subsequently allied himself with five dragons after the death of Ignis in 1040 BF. Someone capable of walking through dragonfire unburned. Someone the Star Spirits' prophecy calls 'the one who cannot burn.'

Daisy's team identified the ice creature fighting Mario as consistent with Fawful's operational signature. They noted that Bowser's forces did not typically include ice-elemental creatures of that description. They correctly reasoned that Bowser might have arrived after the initial attack — not as the perpetrator but as an opportunist, or worse, as someone who had been maneuvered into position.

This analysis, conducted in a bunker in Sarasaland in the first month after the assassination, was more accurate than the official investigation that the Regency controlled for the next eight decades. Waluigi finds this less surprising than it might appear. Official investigations are constrained by what institutions are willing to find. Daisy's bunker team was constrained only by the quality of their intelligence, which was poor, and the analytical capacity of people who had nothing to lose by being right.

The evacuation itself: Daisy moved through the knowledge that her sister was dead with the particular coping mechanism of someone who has learned that grief is a luxury for later. She packed the operational urgency first and left the emotion running underneath it, banked low. The moments when the emotion surfaced — the cracked voice, the hands wrapped around herself, the quiet 'we have to find Mario' pressed against the helicopter window — were moments when the operational urgency momentarily failed to cover what was underneath.

Waluigi notes that Daisy had been in charge of Sarasaland for only four years at the time of the assassination. She had assumed rulership young. The question of whether she was equipped to navigate both an evacuation and a dynastic crisis simultaneously is one she was asking herself, in between managing Pilo T and reviewing satellite feeds from Peach's burning castle. Toadsworth's observation — 'isn't this rash' — was intended as caution. Daisy heard it as doubt, which tells Waluigi something about how she was holding herself together in that helicopter.

She was not rash. She was scared and competent and very young, and she was making correct analytical decisions under conditions of extreme emotional pressure. The Fawful identification was correct. The Bowser-as-scapegoat suspicion was correct. The decision to get herself to safety rather than rush back into a castle where the situation was still active was also correct, even if it felt like cowardice to someone who defines herself as someone who fights rather than runs.

The bunker monitors showed Mario fighting the ice creature. They watched it. They could not help. This is one of the most quietly devastating details in the entire first month — the Princess of Sarasaland, in a secure bunker, watching her brother-in-law fight something large and cold through a satellite feed that could not reach him, because going there would accomplish nothing except adding her to the list of royals who needed to be dealt with.

She stayed in the bunker. It was the right call. It felt terrible. Waluigi respects both things simultaneously.

## Thread Two: Agent T and the Diplomatic Circuit —


The Regency's Reach

Waluigi must be precise about what Agent T represents in this incident record. Agent T was not a rogue operator. Agent T was a Regency agent dispatched during the first month of the post-assassination period to conduct what can only be described as institutional suppression outreach — visiting organizations across the Doughnut World to establish concordants, distribute materials for analysis, and ensure that the institutions best positioned to ask inconvenient questions were either brought inside the Regency's informational framework or made sufficiently compliant through diplomatic agreement.

This is, analytically, the external face of the same cover-up that the Mages' Guild was conducting internally. The Guild eliminated witnesses and controlled evidence. Agent T managed institutional relationships and narrative control in allied and neutral territories. Two prongs of the same operation, running simultaneously during the first month when the cover-up was still wet concrete and needed every available hand to hold it in shape.

Agent T's visit to Baldi's Schoolhouse requires separate treatment and receives it below. The Kivotos visit is the more diplomatically legible of the two threads and Waluigi addresses it first.

The Pony Halo Concordant, as presented to Hanaoka Yuzu of Millennium Science School's Student Council, addressed three stated concerns: preventing the spread of instability from the Mushroom Kingdom to neighboring territories, controlling the movement of persons of interest including Bowser, Koopa Kingdom forces, and Captain Toadette, and establishing border protocols that would limit the movement of non-ponies during a period of diplomatic sensitivity.

Hanaoka's analysis of the concordant was, in Waluigi's assessment, sharper than Agent T had anticipated. She pushed back on the blanket restrictions. She identified the due process concerns. She noted that singling out specific individuals by name — Bowser, Toadette — without evidentiary basis in the concordant itself was legally and ethically problematic. She negotiated a modified version that preserved the security framework while removing the most overreaching provisions.

Waluigi finds this significant for the following reason: Hanaoka was a student council representative at an academic institution. She was not a diplomat, not a lawyer, not a political operative. She was someone who organized event permits and coordinated cultural exchange programs. And she correctly identified the problems with the concordant that a trained Regency diplomat had apparently hoped to slide past her.

This suggests one of two things. Either Agent T underestimated Hanaoka — possible, given that the target was a student — or the concordant was designed to be negotiated down, and the final version was always the intended outcome. Waluigi leans toward the second interpretation. The Pony Halo Concordant's initial terms were extreme enough that any competent counterparty would push back. The modified terms — emergency screening procedures, intelligence sharing, voluntary compliance rather than mandatory restriction — were the actual operational goal. By making the initial terms extreme, Agent T ensured that the final terms felt like a concession when they were actually the plan.

This is sophisticated diplomatic engineering. This is not the work of someone doing routine paperwork during a crisis. This is the work of someone who understood that institutional compliance is more durable than institutional coercion, and who was willing to spend the diplomatic capital of appearing to lose a negotiation in order to achieve the preferred outcome.

Waluigi notes: the Regency was conducting this level of diplomatic sophistication in the first month after the assassination. While eliminating guard witnesses. While controlling the investigation. While managing the evidence chain. Multiple simultaneous operations, all coordinated, all contributing to the same goal of narrative control and institutional compliance.

The cover-up was not improvised. It was planned. Possibly before the assassination. Certainly before the blood was dry.

Momoi's role in the Kivotos thread is analytically minor but humanly significant. A game developer who confused a diplomatic agent for her teacher, who dragged said agent through the school halls to find an adult, who hovered in the student council office while two people negotiated international border policy. She had a sister — no, correction: the detail about a sister working in Peach's kitchens belongs to Molly in the Toadsmith thread. Waluigi is noting the analytical difference between what Momoi knew and what Hanaoka knew. Momoi knew almost nothing. Hanaoka knew only what Agent T told her, which was filtered through the Regency's framework.

Neither of them had access to the journal, the chronicle, the testimony.

They were operating on the surface of events that had an enormous underground structure they could not see.

This is the condition of most people during a cover-up. They are responding to the surface. The Regency managed the surface. The depth was a different matter.

## Thread Three: Baldi and the Vial — Recognition in the Wrong Place


Waluigi will say directly: the Baldi incident is the most analytically troubling of the three threads, and not because Baldi is a particularly significant figure in the post-assassination landscape. He is a schoolteacher. He runs a building. He has a ruler and a pedagogical philosophy that Waluigi finds eccentric but not inherently concerning.

The troubling element is the vial.

Agent T handed Baldi a tube containing a dark liquid with gold pulses moving through it and asked him to analyze it. Baldi analyzed it. He described the liquid as self-motile, light-responsive, non-chemical in structure, and possibly possessing magical resonance consistent with Mages' Guild signature. He reached for a leather-bound notebook that was NOT school-issued — older, with burn marks in the shape of symbols on the cover — and began taking notes in a register that was not academic notation but something more like intelligence documentation.

And then, when Agent T said 'you understand now, don't you,' Baldi stopped writing. He closed the notebook. And he said yes in a voice that was hollow and quiet in a way that stood out because nothing Baldi says is normally hollow and quiet.

Baldi recognized the liquid. Not as an abstract chemical compound requiring academic analysis — he identified it structurally within minutes of first exposure. The self-motile behavior, the light response, the fractals that reformed constantly — he catalogued these not as new observations but as confirmations of something he already knew. The leather notebook with the burn marks suggests prior documentation. Prior documentation of what?

Waluigi has three hypotheses, in order of likelihood:

First: Baldi encountered the liquid, or a similar compound, prior to the assassination. Whether through the Mages' Guild — whose signature he identified in the resonance — or through some independent channel, he had seen this substance before and knew what it was or what it did. His hollow recognition when Agent T confirmed the connection to the assassination suggests the liquid's function is something Baldi considers morally significant. Not merely unusual. Significant in a way that made him go quiet when the pieces connected.

Second: Baldi is or was connected to an intelligence network that predates the Regency's current operations. The leather notebook with burn-mark symbols is not a schoolteacher's research journal. Burn marks in symbolic patterns on leather suggest a document that has been encoded, protected, or initiated in some fashion that goes beyond personal note-taking. Baldi may have been conducting research that connects to the assassination without knowing it connected — or knowing it connected and keeping very careful records.

Third: The liquid is connected to the means of assassination rather than to the conspiracy around it. The four guards who died without wounds, without poison residue, without signs of struggle — killed by simultaneous cessation of all biological function — required a mechanism. A spell, the court mages said. A spell so advanced that fewer than five living practitioners were believed capable of casting it. But what if it was not purely a spell? What if the vector was chemical-magical — a compound applied through some means that left no conventional trace, that would look like magic to magical analysis because it was designed to?

The liquid in the vial is self-motile, light-responsive, structured in reforming fractals. It does not decay. If such a compound could be introduced into an enclosed environment — say, a guard post, through ventilation or contact — the 'simultaneous cessation of all biological function' would not require a powerful spell. It would require a delivery mechanism.

Waluigi is not stating this as fact. Waluigi is stating this as a hypothesis generated by the intersection of Bloomia's testimony about the guards and Baldi's reaction to the liquid. The hypothesis requires more evidence than Waluigi currently possesses. But the intersection is not one Waluigi can ignore.

What Baldi said after recognizing the liquid: nothing further. He went silent. He closed the notebook. He said 'yeah' in one syllable and stopped.

This is the response of someone who has just confirmed something they had suspected and who has decided, in that moment, that confirming it to the person who brought the vial is not safe. Baldi knew something. He confirmed it privately to himself. He did not share the confirmation with Agent T beyond the single syllable.

In the first month of the post-assassination period, with witnesses dying at a rate of one every two to three days, the decision not to share information with a Regency agent is analytically defensible. Baldi had watched the same news reach the same institutions at the same time. He understood what 'my intel could still be bad' meant in practice. He understood what it meant that an agent was traveling the Doughnut World asking people to analyze unusual compounds in the weeks after the assassination.

He said yeah and closed the notebook and Waluigi strongly suspects that notebook is still somewhere, burn-marked and locked, waiting for someone to find it in the right circumstances.

Waluigi intends to find it.

## The Simultaneity — What Three Threads Running at Once Tell Us


Daisy evacuating. Agent T negotiating. Baldi going quiet. All in the same thirty days. All while the Regency was eliminating witnesses, the Mages' Guild was controlling evidence, Toadsworth Sr. was consolidating power, and Toadsmith was finding a journal in an unsorted crate in Bowser's storage wing.

The cover-up did not have the luxury of a still world. It was covering a wound in a living body that was still moving. And a living body that is moving while a wound is being covered tends to bleed through.

Daisy's bunker team bled through the Bowser narrative by identifying Fawful independently. Hanaoka bled through the concordant's initial terms by negotiating them down to what they always should have been. Baldi bled through the isolation of the vial analysis by recognizing something that connected to a knowledge base Agent T did not know he had.

None of these threads resolved the assassination. None of them even came close to the truth in the way that Toadsmith came close, briefly, in the storage wing. But they established, independently and in parallel, that the Regency's control of the narrative was never total. Even in the first thirty days. Even before the Loyalist network existed in any formal sense. Even before anyone had the vocabulary to say 'cover-up' rather than 'investigation.'

People were noticing. Not enough to stop anything. But noticing.

Waluigi finds this simultaneously hopeful and devastating — hopeful because the noticing never entirely stopped, devastating because eighty-five years of noticing did not prevent eighty-five years of the lie continuing.

The difference between noticing and stopping is institutional power. The Regency had it. The people noticing did not. Not in the first month. Not for a long time after.

But Captain Toadette seized Toad Town nine days ago, and the unsigned intelligence note arrived eight days ago, and the Regency's institutional power is cracking for the first time since Highsun 1, 955 BF.

Waluigi is paying attention to the cracks. That is what Waluigi does.

WAH.

threads.narrative:
Princess Daisy received fragmentary intelligence about the assassination and evacuated to a secure bunker via helicopter piloted by Pilo T — a pilot she correctly identified as unreliable and trusted anyway because reliable options were not available. The evacuation was operationally sound even when it felt like cowardice. In the bunker, Daisy's tactical staff reviewed satellite feeds showing Mario fighting an ice creature consistent with Fawful's operational signature — not Bowser's standard forces. The team independently developed the hypothesis that Bowser had arrived after the initial attack rather than as the perpetrator, which placed them ahead of the official investigation that the Regency was simultaneously constructing around the Bowser-as-assassin narrative.

The intelligence Daisy acted on was incomplete and possibly corrupted by the Regency's information management. She did not know about the hatch, the journal, the guard rotation gap, or Bloomia's leather case. She knew only what had escaped the capital in the chaos of the first hours, filtered through channels that the Regency was already beginning to control.

She was still more right than the official investigation would be for eighty-five years.

threads.title: Agent T, the Pony Halo Concordant, and the Regency's Institutional Outreach During the Active Cover-Up
threads.date: Approximately Highsun 5–22, 955 BF (overlapping with Toadsmith Incident)
threads.location: Kivotos — Millennium Science School / Multiple Doughnut World Institutions
threads.narrative:
A Regency agent identified as Agent T conducted a diplomatic circuit across multiple Doughnut World institutions during the first month of the post-assassination period, ostensibly to maintain stability and pony-student relations during a time of crisis. The stated concerns — preventing instability spread, controlling persons of interest including Bowser and Captain Toadette, establishing border protocols — were the surface layer of an operation whose actual function was institutional compliance management.

At Millennium Science School in Kivotos, Agent T was initially received by Saiba Momoi of the Game Development Club, who had mistaken them for her teacher. Momoi escorted Agent T to the Student Council office, where Hanaoka Yuzu received them with composed professionalism that exceeded what a student council representative might have been expected to provide.

The Pony Halo Concordant as initially presented included extreme provisions: blanket restrictions on Mushroom Kingdom citizens, named persons of interest including Bowser and Captain Toadette, and border protocols more restrictive than Kivotos's standard institutional framework. Hanaoka pushed back methodically — identifying due process concerns, the discrimination risks of nationality-based restriction, and the ethical problems of singling out individuals by name without evidentiary basis in the concordant itself.

The final negotiated version was modified: emergency screening rather than blanket exclusion, voluntary intelligence sharing rather than mandatory compliance, flexibility for approved exchanges with security clearance. A version that Hanaoka could accept without violating her institution's principles.

Waluigi's assessment: the initial terms were designed to be negotiated down. The modified terms were the actual operational goal. Institutional compliance achieved through apparent concession is more durable than institutional compliance achieved through coercion, because the complying party believes they have protected their principles when they have in fact agreed to the framework that was always intended. The Regency obtained what it wanted. Hanaoka believed she had protected Kivotos. Both things are true simultaneously.
key_analytical_points: The diplomatic circuit was the external face of the same cover-up the Mages' Guild was conducting internally — two simultaneous operations serving the same goal
The concordant's initial extreme terms were almost certainly designed to be negotiated down to the actual intended outcome
Hanaoka's competence as a negotiator exceeded what Agent T had apparently anticipated — or the underestimation was itself part of the design

Momoi's role as an accidental intermediary is humanly significant even if analytically minor — she represents the class of people who are adjacent to enormous events without any visibility into their actual nature

The Regency conducting sophisticated diplomatic engineering simultaneously with witness elimination and evidence control indicates the cover-up was coordinated at a level that precludes improvisation — this was planned

threads.name: Thread Three: Baldi and the Vial
threads.title: What the Schoolteacher Recognized, Why He Went Silent, and What the Vial Might Actually Be
threads.location: Baldi's Schoolhouse (Valley of Bowser Adjacent / Neutral Territory)
threads.narrative:
Agent T visited Baldi's Schoolhouse during the diplomatic circuit and, after initial introductions established the nature of the visit, presented a tube containing a dark liquid with self-motile gold pulses moving through its interior. The liquid was asked to be analyzed.

Baldi's analysis was methodical and rapid. He identified the liquid as self-motile, light-responsive, non-chemical in structure, and possessing magical resonance consistent with Mages' Guild signature. He produced a leather-bound notebook with burn marks in symbolic patterns on the cover — not a school-issue document — and began recording observations in a register that read more like intelligence documentation than academic notation.

The observations: self-motile behavior, light response, non-chemical structure, possible magical resonance. Under magnification, the particles formed tiny reforming fractals — mathematical structures that twisted and reformed constantly, described by Baldi as 'mathematics given form, or the opposite of math entirely: chaos with purpose.'

When Agent T confirmed the connection to the assassination — 'you understand now, don't you' — Baldi stopped writing. Closed the notebook. Said 'yeah' in a single syllable and did not elaborate.

This response is the analytically significant element. Not the analysis itself — competent, rapid, more thorough than expected — but the moment when recognition arrived and Baldi chose silence. He had identified something. He confirmed it to himself. He did not share the confirmation with Agent T beyond the bare minimum acknowledgment that he understood.

In the first month of the post-assassination period, with witnesses dying at a predictable rate, choosing not to share confirmed information with a Regency agent is a survival decision. Baldi made it in the same moment he made the recognition, which suggests the recognition and the assessment of risk arrived together. He knew what the liquid was, and he knew that knowing it in front of Agent T was dangerous.

Waluigi's three hypotheses about the liquid:

First: The liquid is connected to the mechanism that killed the four guards — simultaneous cessation of all biological function, no wounds, no poison residue, no signs of struggle. Court mages attributed this to a spell of extreme sophistication. But the liquid's properties — self-motile, light-responsive, non-decaying, structured in reforming fractals — are consistent with a compound designed to evade conventional chemical detection while delivering a magical-biological payload. If introduced into an enclosed environment through contact or ventilation, such a compound could produce the guard deaths without requiring a practitioner of exceptional skill to be physically present.

Second: The liquid has a prior documented history that includes Baldi's prior encounter with it or with a similar compound, predating the assassination. The burn-marked notebook suggests this documentation exists.

Third: The liquid is connected to the Mages' Guild in a way that is not simply a matter of magical resonance — it may be a Guild-manufactured compound, produced for the specific purpose of the assassination and now being circulated for 'analysis' by an Agent who wanted confirmation from someone outside the Guild's institutional framework.

The third hypothesis, if correct, makes Agent T's visit to Baldi particularly alarming. Why would the Regency want external confirmation of a Guild compound's properties? Either to verify that the compound was performing as designed, to assess how identifiable it was to non-Guild analysts, or to determine whether Baldi's prior knowledge of the compound could be confirmed and therefore managed.

Baldi went silent. He has not been heard from on this matter since. The notebook with the burn marks has not surfaced in any subsequent record available to Waluigi.
key_analytical_points: Baldi's rapid identification of the liquid's properties suggests prior familiarity — the analysis read as confirmation rather than discovery
The leather notebook with burn-mark symbols is not a schoolteacher's research tool — it represents a documentation practice that predates and exceeds Baldi's stated academic role
The choice of silence at the moment of recognition indicates simultaneous arrival of the recognition and the risk assessment — Baldi knew what it was and knew that saying so was dangerous

The liquid's properties — self-motile, non-decaying, fractally structured, light-responsive — are consistent with a compound designed to evade conventional detection while delivering a biological payload

The intersection of these properties with the guard deaths — simultaneous, painless, no conventional evidence — generates a hypothesis that the 'spell' attribution may have been cover for a chemical-magical delivery mechanism
Baldi's subsequent silence mirrors the silence of the guard witnesses who survived briefly and then disappeared — though in his case it appears to have been voluntary rather than enforced
The burn-marked notebook represents a potential evidence thread that Waluigi intends to pursue

name: The Toadsmith Incident
title: What Sir Toadsmith the Third Found in Bowser's Filing Cabinet, and Why He Stopped Answering Questions
date: Approximately Highsun 22, 955 BF — three weeks after the assassination
location: Bowser's Castle (Valley of Bowser) / Valley of Bowser Maintenance Tunnels / Donut Plains Neutral Settlement
type: Active Investigation / Evidence Recovery / Covert Sabotage / Accidental Discovery of Things the Investigation Was Designed Not to Find
status: Partially Resolved — journal recovered, valley destabilized, Toadsmith went dark twenty-one days after the assassination and six days after the last guard witness disappeared
note: Waluigi has reconstructed this incident from three sources: a partial debrief from Toadsmith himself, filed through channels that would not become formally Loyalist for another twenty-five years but which were already being used by people who had started asking questions the Regency preferred unasked; the valley collapse report issued by Bowser's engineering staff, which documents the structural damage without identifying a cause; and an unsigned intelligence note that arrived at Waluigi's location by courier with no return address, containing details that only someone present inside Bowser's Castle on Highsun 22 could have known. Waluigi received this note in 1040 BF — eighty-five years after the events it describes. Someone held this information for eighty-five years and chose NOW to share it. Waluigi does not know who. Waluigi does not know why now. Waluigi suspects both answers are connected to the fact that Captain Toadette seized Toad Town nine days ago and the Regency's hold on its own narrative is cracking for the first time since the assassination. People share secrets when the structure protecting those secrets begins to fail. The timing is not coincidental. The timing is never coincidental. WAH.
summary: Three weeks after Princess Peach was murdered on Highsun 1, 955 BF — while the kingdom was still in formal mourning, while the investigation was still nominally active, while the last guard witness had vanished only six days prior and Bloomia's disappearance was barely a week old — a Regency investigator named Sir Toadsmith the Third was dispatched to Bowser's Castle to conduct a formal interview regarding Bowser's invasion on the night of the assassination. The assignment was routine. The blade evidence had already been placed in the official record. The interview was procedural documentation — a paper trail establishing that the Regency had pursued the Koopa angle through proper channels while the actual cover-up continued in the background. Toadsmith was the proper channel. He did not know this. He walked into Bowser's throne room carrying planted evidence he believed was real, asked questions he had been given by people who already knew the answers, and stumbled into a confiscated property vault containing a journal in Peach's handwriting that contradicted everything the Regency was building. The journal established that Peach had known about the conspiracy for months, that the Koopa-forged blade had been sourced internally rather than from Koopa forces, that a figure she called 'the engineer' had been coordinating with her before her death, and that what happened on Highsun 1 was not an assassination in the conventional sense but something far more difficult to categorize. Toadsmith also encountered forces operating inside Bowser's Castle that were not Bowser's — forces consistent with Eggman's private security apparatus, present in the castle three weeks after the assassination and targeting specific confiscated materials. Toadsmith escaped through the Valley of Bowser's maintenance tunnels with three civilian volunteers, triggered a structural collapse that compromised six tunnel systems and redirected a lava tube, reached Donut Plains, disclosed fragments of the journal's contents to approximately forty witnesses in a market square — where a former Royal Scribe confirmed the handwriting as genuine — and then went silent. He has not been heard from since. The cover-up continued. The lie solidified. And the journal sat with a Donut Plains elder for eighty-five years while the kingdom burned.
description:
Waluigi needs to establish the context in which the Toadsmith Incident occurred, because the context is what makes it significant. Three weeks is not a long time. Three weeks after a princess is murdered is a period when everything is still raw, still moving, still being decided. The narrative has not calcified yet. The institutions have not fully closed around the conspiracy. The people who know things are still alive — most of them — and the people who are eliminating the people who know things are still working through their list.

On Highsun 22, 955 BF — the approximate date of the Toadsmith Incident — the following were true:

Bloomia had disappeared eight days earlier, on Highsun 14. The official explanation — 'personal reasons' — had been issued but was already generating uncomfortable questions among palace staff who knew that handmaidens do not leave their posts during a national crisis for personal reasons. Nobody was saying this publicly. Several people were thinking it.

Two of the three perimeter guard witnesses were dead. Corporal Redspot had 'fallen from a tower' on Day 5. Sergeant Brownshield had 'choked at dinner' on Day 6. Captain Silvercap had vanished on Day 7. The investigation had three witnesses who could testify about the guard rotation gap and all three were gone within a week. This is not a coincidence rate that any competent investigator accepts as coincidence. But the investigation was not being run by competent investigators. It was being run by the Mages' Guild, who had assumed control on Day 7 — the same day Captain Silvercap vanished — citing jurisdictional concerns regarding magical evidence.

Toadsworth the Elder had been named Acting Regent on Day 9. His private journals — which would not be recovered for another fifty-five years — reference 'the arrangement' in entries from this period. He was consolidating power while the kingdom mourned. He was converting a tragedy into a transition. And he was doing it with the full cooperation of the Mages' Guild, whose tall mage Valorian Stormweave had been seen exchanging instructions with Toadsworth in the hours after the assassination.

The Koopa-forged blade had been introduced into the evidence chain within the first forty-eight hours. Where it came from, who placed it, and how it entered the investigation record are questions that the official process never addressed because the official process was not designed to address them. The blade was there. It was Koopa-forged. That was sufficient for the narrative being constructed.

Bowser's invasion of the castle on the night of the assassination was documented, real, and convenient. He had invaded. His forces had seized materials. He had been repelled by the Toad Guard reinforced by — notably — Mages' Guild combat units who arrived with suspicious speed. Bowser's invasion gave the conspiracy its scapegoat. Whether the invasion was provoked, anticipated, or simply exploited is a question Waluigi cannot fully resolve from available evidence. What is clear is that someone needed an external enemy to blame, and Bowser — who had a documented history of invading Peach's castle — was the obvious candidate.

Into this environment, three weeks after the murder, with the cover-up still under active construction, Sir Toadsmith the Third was sent to interview the scapegoat.

## The


Assignment — What Toadsmith Was Actually Sent to Do

The official assignment: conduct a formal interview with Bowser regarding the Koopa-forged blade and Bowser's presence at the castle on Highsun 1.

Waluigi's analytical assessment: the assignment was procedural cover. The blade evidence was already in the official record. The interview was designed to generate documentation — a paper trail showing the Regency had formally pursued the Bowser angle, so that when the narrative calcified into established history, it would include the notation that the suspect had been interviewed and the investigation had been thorough.

This is how institutional cover-ups work in their early phases. You do not simply suppress the truth. You generate so much official-looking documentation around the lie that the lie acquires the weight and texture of legitimate process. The interview was not investigative. It was decorative. A piece of institutional furniture designed to make the room look like an office rather than a crime scene.

Toadsmith was selected because he was competent, procedural, and unlikely to deviate from his briefing materials. Waluigi has reviewed what is known of Toadsmith's career — limited documentation, but consistent with a mid-rank investigator who followed protocols, filed paperwork correctly, and did not ask questions that exceeded his assignment parameters. This is the profile of someone who is useful to institutions that want things done properly without things being done thoroughly. There is a difference. The Regency understood this difference. Toadsmith, at the time of his assignment, did not.

The question of whether Toadsmith knew the blade was planted is analytically significant. Waluigi's position: he did not. The blade was in the official evidence record. His briefing materials referenced it as established fact. If you embed a deception into the baseline documentation deeply enough, every investigator who works from that documentation perpetuates the deception without knowing they are doing so. This is more efficient than conspiracy. Conspiracy requires participants who know what they are doing. Institutional documentation management requires only participants who trust their own files.

Waluigi finds this more disturbing than deliberate malice, because deliberate malice at least acknowledges the existence of the truth it is suppressing. Documentation management simply makes the truth invisible to people who are looking at the wrong documents.

## The


Interview — What Happened in the Throne Room

Bowser's Castle in the Valley of Bowser was, three weeks after the assassination, in a state of agitated fortification. The Valley itself — a subterranean volcanic landscape carved by ancient lava flows, accessible through a massive rock carving of Bowser's own face rising from the sea, lightning perpetually flickering in the cavern sky — was on high alert. Bowser's forces had been repelled from Peach's castle. The Regency was publicly accusing Bowser of the assassination. Bowser was publicly denying it. The kingdom was in mourning. And Bowser — who had invaded the castle to kidnap Peach, not to kill her, and who had arrived to find her already dead — was in a state that his staff later described as 'volcanic fury with nowhere to direct itself.'

Bowser received Toadsmith in the throne room. The choice of venue was characteristically Bowser — a massive chamber designed to emphasize the scale differential between the eight-foot Koopa King and any non-Koopa visitor. The torches flared orange-red. The ceiling was high enough to be lost in shadow. The doors shut behind Toadsmith loudly, and by the time he turned to check if they had locked, Bowser was already laughing behind him.

The interview began conventionally: credentials presented, questions asked, theatrical displays of offense performed. Bowser played the part of the affronted king — boisterous, dismissive, gesturing broadly at his own legacy of dramatic invasion as evidence that he was a kidnapper, not a murderer. There is honor in conquest, he said. Bowser doesn't kill princesses.

Toadsmith introduced the Koopa-forged blade.

Bowser went still. The theatrics dropped. His voice flattened. Smoke stopped curling from his nostrils. He said: 'You don't just say that name unless you've seen it or touched it.'

Waluigi has three observations about this response that have not changed since the first version of this entry and will not change:

First: Bowser called it a 'name,' not a weapon. The blade has a specific identity in Koopa knowledge. It is not a generic weapon attributed to Koopa forces — it is a particular object known to Bowser personally. Secret Koopa magic, as he put it. Passed down from the First King. A handful of people know it exists.

Second: The cold replacement of performance with genuine reaction indicates the blade question reached something real. Bowser performs constantly. The laughter, the chest-puffing, the dramatic declarations — these are the armor of a king who has learned that presence is power. When that armor drops and the voice flattens and the smoke stops, the subject has been touched somewhere the performance does not cover.

Third: 'Unless you've seen it or touched it' implies restricted, experiential knowledge. This blade is not publicly known. Someone brought it into the investigation from a controlled information environment. Toadsmith had seen neither. He had read the briefing materials, which contained the blade's name as established fact. When he said the name to Bowser, he was reading from a document he trusted. He did not know why the name produced the reaction it produced.

Bowser did not attack. He demanded to know who told Toadsmith the name. When Toadsmith refused to disclose the source — correctly, procedurally, by the book — Bowser's suspicion shifted from Toadsmith to his own inner circle. Someone inside the castle had been talking. He slammed a gauntlet onto his fist, kicked open a massive iron door, and declared that every guard on duty the night of the assassination was getting questioned one by one.

Toadsmith followed him. This is documented in the debrief as a choice, not a compulsion. Toadsmith chose to follow because the interview was deviating from his briefing in ways that suggested Bowser had information the briefing had not anticipated. A procedural investigator who follows protocols would have left. Toadsmith stayed. This is the first moment in the record where Toadsmith behaved like an investigator rather than a documentation asset.

## The Security Chamber — What the Footage Showed


Bowser led Toadsmith to a security monitoring chamber: walls covered in glowing screens showing footage from every corner of the castle. Six guards sat at attention and rose instantly when Bowser entered. The Koopa King's tail whipped through the air — the guards flinched — and he slammed his fist on the console without preamble.

The footage rolled. Time stamp: 23:47, the night of the assassination.

Peach was in her throne room. Not dead. Not struggling. Sitting calmly with a cup of tea, a slight smile on her face as though enjoying the quiet. Then: movement in the doorway. A hooded figure, smaller than Bowser's silhouette, moving without aggression. The guards in the footage did not react. No alarms. No challenge. The figure approached Peach's throne and knelt.

Peach set down her teacup. She nodded at the figure like they were expected.

The hooded figure reached up — not to attack — and handed her something small and metallic. A glint of silver caught the camera. Smooth, engraved, clearly not a standard weapon.

Bowser froze the frame. He jabbed a claw at the screen.

Not one of his troops. Not a Toad. Not anyone on the Mushroom Kingdom uniform roster he had reviewed the previous week. The figure's walk was distinctive — stiff shoulders, a particular bearing — and the glove on the outstretched hand bore a small emblem: a silver bolt stitched in the fabric, fingerless design, initials E.M. visible on the inner seam.

One of the guards cleared his throat. He produced a patrol log notebook and flipped to a page covered in messy notes and margin sketches. He pointed to a small drawing: an ornate pendant matching what appeared on screen. He said he had seen the symbol carved into a wall panel in the old west tower, covered in ivy and dust, during reconstruction after Bowser Jr.'s birthday party explosion. The man who came to inspect the repairs — hooded, same bearing, same gloves — had worn something like it. The guard said the name quietly, as though saying it too loudly might summon something:

Dr. Eggman.

Bowser laughed. Not the theatrical performative laugh — a genuine, thunderous, belly-deep laugh of a king who has just learned something that is simultaneously absurd and enraging. Eggman? In his castle? Without his knowledge? Disguised with a cloak and apparently trusting that no one would recognize his personal embroidery?

The laughter stopped when Bowser looked back at the screen and noticed what Toadsmith had already noticed: Peach's face when she received the object was not afraid. It was not surprised. It was the face of someone receiving something they had been waiting for.

## The SOS Signal and What It Summoned


At some point during the security chamber review — the debrief is not specific about the exact moment — Toadsmith pressed a concealed device in his pocket. Standard Regency procedure: an SOS signal to be received by backup, triggering a reinforcement response.

The signal was sent. It was not received by Regency backup.

This is the part of the incident that Waluigi finds most clarifying. Toadsmith's SOS went out and Eggman's private security forces arrived at Bowser's Castle within hours, descending via helicopter toward the storage wing where confiscated Peach materials were held. A sleek black-and-red aircraft with Eggman's silver bolt insignia on the side. Dark-armored figures leaping out before the landing gear fully settled. Moving with the efficiency of people who knew exactly where they were going and what they were looking for.

The signal was either intercepted or the storage wing was already a target. The witness elimination timeline was not abstract to him at this point — Redspot on Day 5, Brownshield on Day 6, Silvercap on Day 7, Bloomia on Day 14. He ran.

## The Storage Wing — What Was in the Crate


Toadsmith did not run directly for the exit. The debrief documents a decision that Waluigi considers either extraordinarily brave or catastrophically impractical depending on one's tolerance for investigative risk: he ran toward the storage wing.

Not toward Eggman's forces. Through the servant passages, the narrow spiral staircases, the forgotten storage halls that Bowser had never bothered to patrol because they contained only broken chairs and rusted armor and barrels labeled 'Not Explosives' that almost certainly were. Toadsmith moved through the parts of the castle nobody was watching because nobody important was supposed to be there.

He found the crate labeled CONFISCATED in jagged red paint.

Inside: a tangle of wires, a small backpack with Mushroom Kingdom insignias marked officially missing in the inventory records, and a leather-bound journal with 'Peach' written on the cover in elegant script. Faded from handling. The corners worn. The leather creased along the spine in the particular way of a book that has been opened and closed many times by the same careful hands.

It had been sitting in that crate for three weeks. Three weeks during which the Mages' Guild was systematically eliminating witnesses, Toadsworth Sr. was consolidating power, and the official narrative was being constructed around the blade. Three weeks during which the single most important piece of contradictory evidence — Peach's own words, in her own handwriting — was sitting in an unsorted crate in the castle of the man being framed for her murder.

Toadsmith read it. Not all of it — Eggman's forces were in the storage wing above him and he was aware that the time available for literary appreciation was limited. But he read enough.

The entries, reconstructed from Toadsmith's debrief:

Entry one, approximately three weeks before the assassination — six weeks before the Toadsmith Incident. Peach references contact from the engineer. 'Everything is in place.' The blade will appear 'in the right hands at the right time.' She does not know if the engineer means to protect her or to bury someone else.

Waluigi must stop here. Because in light of what the Coronation Day manuscript establishes — that Peach chose her death, that she sat at her vanity and waited, that she prepared a leather case with documents and a pendant and sent Bloomia to run — the phrase 'everything is in place' is not the language of a victim being warned. It is the language of a strategist receiving a status update. The engineer was not telling her what was coming. He was confirming that the preparations she had requested were complete. The blade's placement. The evidence chain. The scapegoat narrative. These were components of a plan being confirmed to a participant, not threats being described to a target.

This reframes the engineer entirely. He was not an intelligence asset warning a princess in danger. He was an operational partner executing a plan that Peach herself had designed or co-designed. The plan required that she die. The plan required that the death look like assassination. The plan required a scapegoat — Bowser, whose documented history of invasion made him the obvious candidate — and the plan required that the truth eventually emerge, carried by someone young enough to survive and loyal enough to run.

The leather case behind the loose stone. The documents. Bloomia.

Peach prepared all of it because the plan included her own death and the eventual exposure of the conspiracy that her death was designed to reveal.

Entry two, approximately two weeks before the assassination. The engineer visited in person. He came through the hatch — the same hatch that the assassin would later use, the same passage that Bowser's forces found when they arrived and discovered Peach's body. The engineer came through the lover's entrance because he either was the lover, knew the lover, or had been told about the entrance by Peach herself. He delivered the silver key. He told her 'Bowser is not the enemy and neither is he.' He told her 'the enemy has been in the room with me every day for thirty years and I have been too kind to see it.'

Thirty years. Peach had reigned for thirty-two years before the assassination. Thirty years places the enemy's presence at approximately 923 BF, two years into her reign. Toadsworth Sr. became Chamberlain in 924 BF. The Mages' Guild established its investigative jurisdiction in 925 BF. The institutional infrastructure that would eventually enable the conspiracy was built in exactly this period. The enemy was not someone who arrived. The enemy was someone who was always there, whose thirty-year proximity had made them invisible in the way that furniture is invisible — always present, never examined.

Someone Peach saw every day.

Someone she had been too kind to see clearly.

Entry three, approximately one week before the assassination. Peach confirms the blade is genuinely Koopa-forged but was 'given to the engineer by someone inside the investigation, not someone inside Bowser's forces.' The blade was sourced internally. Given to the engineer by someone with access to both Koopa weapon fabrication and the investigative apparatus. In the three-week timeline, the 'investigation' referenced cannot be the post-assassination investigation — it is the pre-assassination preparation. The investigation was not corrupted after the fact. It was corrupted before the murder happened.

The people who would investigate the crime were part of the crime before it was committed.

The Chronicles' cipher says it plainly: 'THE GUILD PROVIDED THE BLADE.' The Mages' Guild sourced a Koopa-forged weapon and provided it to the engineer, who confirmed this to Peach. The blade was never Koopa evidence. It was Guild evidence dressed in Koopa manufacturing, placed in the official record within forty-eight hours of the assassination by people who had been holding it for exactly this purpose.

Final entry, the day before the assassination. 'I am not afraid. I am sad that I cannot be more forthcoming. The people I love are being used as instruments by people who will be pleased when I am gone.'

In the context of Coronation Day — where Bloomia establishes that Peach chose her death, chose her killer, sat at her vanity and waited — this is not the farewell of a helpless victim. It is the farewell of a strategist executing the last move of a plan that requires her own removal from the board. 'The people I love are being used as instruments.' Thornpaw's secret relationship was leverage held over him. Bloomia's youth and loyalty made her the ideal evidence carrier. The guards whose deaths would follow were the conspiracy's cleanup. And Peach, sitting at the center of it all, was managing her own assassination with the same political precision that had characterized thirty-two years of reign.

She was not murdered. She was coronated. Again. For the last time.

## The Escape — Through the Castle, Down the Cliff,


Into the Valley

Toadsmith closed the journal, tucked it under his arm, and moved the chair.

The storage room had one window: narrow, high on the far wall, unbarred. He stacked a barrel under a chair for extra height, climbed up, grabbed the stone ledge, and looked out.

The Valley of Bowser spread below him in volcanic layers — brown and black cliffs carved by ancient lava flows, twisted garbage piles across the wasteland floor where Munchers scavenged through refuse, Dino-Torches flickering near cave entrances in the distance. The lightning that perpetually illuminates the valley's cavern sky flashed in the background, briefly revealing the silhouette of Bowser's Koopa Clown Car on the castle roof before darkness swallowed it again. High. High enough that one wrong step would end the investigation permanently.

But a maintenance trail wound down the cliff face from this section of the castle — a narrow ledge of stone with vines clinging to it, used by servants or engineers, slanting toward the valley floor. And at the trail's end: a warp pipe entrance, half-buried in dirt, covered in vines, marked with the yellow-and-blue spiral pattern of Donut Plains. The secret passage. The exit that bypassed the front doors, bypassed the guards, bypassed everything.

Toadsmith considered the Clown Car on the roof. Fast. Enclosed. No climbing. He dismissed it immediately — Bowser would notice within minutes and the pursuit would be immediate and fiery.

He swung his leg over the ledge, clutched the journal to his chest, and began climbing down.

Behind him, in the castle: chaos had arrived. Eggman's forces had breached the storage wing. Bowser had found them. The resulting collision — a Koopa King in volcanic fury encountering an elite paramilitary unit that had invaded his home without invitation — produced explosions visible from the cliff face, plasma bolts crackling through the torchlit hallways, and at least one impact massive enough to crack a section of interior wall that shook dust down onto Toadsmith's hat as he descended.

Good. Everyone who might notice a small Toad on a maintenance trail was occupied with something much louder.

He reached the boulder cluster halfway down, ducked into the gap between two moss-covered rocks, and watched the helicopter. Black-and-red, Eggman's silver bolt logo on the side, rotors with that distinctive uneven thump-thump-thump that Regency security briefings had flagged as Eggman's personal aircraft signature. It had descended toward the storage wing, deposited its forces, and now hovered in a holding pattern — waiting for retrieval or for signal.

They were going to find the crate open. The journal missing. Someone had been there.

Toadsmith moved.

He reached the warp pipe entrance at the valley floor — half-buried, vine-covered, the spiral tile glowing faintly when his foot touched it. He stepped onto it fully. The ancient magic activated. Colors smeared. Wind rushed from nowhere. The Valley of Bowser, the lightning, the volcanic rock, the distant sound of Bowser's roar — all of it stretched and vanished.

He landed on soft grass in sunlight.

Donut Plains. Rolling hills, flower fields, candy clouds drifting in a gentle breeze. Birds. A marketplace in the distance. A cozy Toad Town between two hills with smoke curling from chimneys.

Safe ground. Neutral territory. A place with no Regency garrison, no Mages' Guild presence, no Eggman operation.

A place with witnesses.

## The Three Volunteers — Who Helped and Why


Toadsmith did not reach Donut Plains alone in the sense of having no assistance. The debrief references three civilians recruited in the settlement after his arrival but before his public disclosure — people who helped him navigate the final stage of the operation and who were present for the tunnel work.

Molly: a mechanic. Controlled demolition expertise. She had worked mining contracts in the valley's outer tunnels before the border tensions made that work unviable. She knew the structural geography of the maintenance passages. She agreed to help, according to the debrief, because she had a sister who worked in Peach's castle kitchens and had not been heard from since the assassination. She wanted to know if the things Toadsmith was saying were true. She helped make the tunnels collapse as partial payment for the answer.

Gus: a miner. Structural assessment. He had spent twenty years reading lava flow patterns and geological stress indicators in various kingdoms' tunnel systems. He was the one who identified which supports to compromise for maximum cascade effect. He was also the one who said, at the relevant moment, that the chain reaction might exceed intended scope given the active lava tube running adjacent to the eastern passage. Toadsmith noted this concern in the debrief. He proceeded anyway because the alternative was not proceeding, and not proceeding meant Eggman's forces had time to seal the valley and cut off the exit.

Vance: a retired guard. He had served in Donut Plains' local militia before the Regency centralized security under the Mages' Guild and made local militias largely ceremonial. He handled rear security during the escape. He had opinions about the Mages' Guild that the debrief describes as 'extensive' and which Toadsmith apparently did not have time to fully document.

All three returned safely to Donut Plains. Toadsmith did not return with them.

## The Valley Collapse — Six Tunnels and a Redirected Lava Tube


The tunnel collapse was not about provoking a war. Waluigi wants to be precise about this because the valley collapse report issued by Bowser's engineering corps has been used by subsequent analysts to suggest that the sabotage was designed to escalate Mushroom Kingdom-Koopa tensions. It was not. It was designed to make Bowser too visible, too politically present, too much of a public figure to simply eliminate.

In the three-week timeline, the witness elimination pattern was still active. Redspot Day 5, Brownshield Day 6, Silvercap Day 7, Bloomia Day 14. The rate suggests one to three days between eliminations once a target was identified. Toadsmith had been inside Bowser's Castle, had encountered Eggman's forces, had taken the journal, and had escaped. He was now a witness who had direct physical evidence contradicting the official narrative. By the pattern, he had two to three days before someone came looking.

If the Regency wanted to maintain the Bowser-as-assassin narrative, they needed Bowser alive long enough for the narrative to solidify — a dead Bowser with an unresolved blame structure was politically complicated. But a Bowser whose valley was having geological incidents, whose territory was drawing diplomatic attention from neighboring regions, whose resources were occupied with infrastructure crisis rather than sitting quietly while the cover-up completed — that Bowser was harder to quietly manage. You cannot conduct a clean political operation against someone who is already the center of attention.

Molly's controlled demolition expertise was substantial in stable mining environments. It was less applicable to chain reactions in geologically active lava systems. Gus had flagged this. The eastern passage collapse triggered secondary stress fractures in two adjacent tunnels. The lava tube redirection was unintended. Six total tunnel systems were compromised. Local agriculture in the valley's eastern agricultural patches was affected for several growing seasons. Nobody was killed immediately, though the secondary consequences unfolded over months in ways that the engineering report documents without identifying a cause.

The report concluded geological instability. The valley has genuine instability — lightning-lit cavern sky, active lava flows, the particular geological character of a volcanic region accessed through a subterranean cavern carved in the shape of its ruler's face. Nobody looked for saboteurs because nobody saw saboteurs, and the physical evidence was consistent with natural cascade events in the relevant rock formations.

The sabotage has never been attributed to Toadsmith. Bowser never knew a Regency investigator blew up six of his tunnels on the way out.

Waluigi finds this almost funny. Almost.

## The Public Disclosure — Forty Witnesses and a Scribe Who Remembered


Toadsmith reached the Donut Plains market square and climbed onto the platform beside the town crier. The crowd turned. Conversations stopped. A baker dropped a cake on the cobblestones and did not notice it splatter. Children started crying, picking up the gravity from adult faces before they had words for it.

Toadsmith held up the journal — the cover marked 'Peach' in elegant script, visible from the front rows — and said, loudly enough for the square to hear:

'Princess Peach was murdered. And she knew about it before it happened.'

The gasps, the whispers, the hats clutched and mouths covered — these are documented in two independent sources, both of which describe the crowd's response in terms suggesting that most people present already half-believed something was wrong but had not had language for it yet. Toadsmith gave them language.

The elder stepped forward. A wise-looking Toad with glasses, described in the debrief as 'the kind of person who has spent a lifetime being more careful with words than most people are with swords.' He identified himself as Peach's former Royal Scribe — ten years of service, Toadsmith notes, which in the three-week timeline means his expertise is current professional knowledge rather than decades-old memory. He examined the cover. He asked where Toadsmith had found it. He flipped to the first page — a small doodle of Peach's signature flower, 'Private' written beneath in delicate script — and looked up at the crowd.

He confirmed it. The handwriting was genuine. He would stake his reputation on it. He had written beside that hand for a decade and you do not forget it.

Forty people heard this. Forty people in a neutral settlement without Regency garrison or courier service or institutional infrastructure.

The Regency could suppress the journal. They could seize a physical object, burn a leather book, eliminate a paper trail. They could not suppress the memory of forty people who watched a former Royal Scribe confirm the handwriting of a dead princess in a market square on a sunny afternoon in Donut Plains.

Information does not need institutions to travel. It needs people who talk to other people. The core facts — Peach knew, the blade was planted, someone called the engineer warned her — entered the regional rumor network and began the slow migration toward what would eventually become the Loyalist intelligence framework. Every subsequent thread of the investigation that would continue for eighty-five years traces back to this moment, not because Toadsmith discovered everything — he did not — but because he proved, three weeks into the active construction of the cover-up, that the cover-up had cracks.

The elder received the physical journal for safekeeping. The elder is almost certainly dead by now. The journal's chain of custody across eighty-five years is unknown to Waluigi and is a thread he intends to pull.

## Toadsmith's Fate — What the Debrief Suggests


Toadsmith filed one debrief through channels that would later become the Loyalist dead drop network. In 955 BF, these channels were informal — sympathetic individuals who passed information to each other because they had started asking questions that the Regency preferred unasked. The network that Captain Toadette would formalize decades later began as a loose association of people who noticed things and did not like what they noticed.

The debrief was complete. Procedurally formatted. Containing what he saw, what he found, the key contents of the journal, and enough structural detail for reconstruction by a later analyst. It reads like documentation prepared by someone who knew they might not be available for follow-up questions. Someone who was writing for an audience they would never meet, making sure that audience would have what they needed.

After the debrief: nothing. He did not return to Donut Plains. Molly, Gus, and Vance returned. Toadsmith did not return with them. He went dark on approximately Day 21 — six days after the last guard witness vanished, eight days after Bloomia disappeared.

Waluigi's assessment of possible outcomes, in order of likelihood:

Most likely: Toadsmith went to ground voluntarily. He understood the witness elimination pattern because the journal gave him the framework to see it clearly. He filed the debrief to ensure the information survived and then disappeared into whatever resources he could access or improvise. The debrief's completeness supports this interpretation — it is the work of a man who has made his peace with the possibility that he cannot be a continuing source and has therefore made himself a complete one.

Less likely but possible: Toadsmith was taken. By Regency operatives who identified his use of the informal channels. By the engineer's forces, who had demonstrated both the capability and the motivation. By some third party whose interests Waluigi cannot fully map. In the three-week timeline, the number of parties actively hunting inconvenient witnesses is larger and more aggressive than it would be later, when the cover-up was complete and cleanup was no longer urgent.

Least likely but not dismissible: something happened in the tunnels that the debrief does not cover. Gus had flagged the chain reaction risk. Molly's expertise had limits in active lava systems. The debrief was filed from Donut Plains, which means Toadsmith survived long enough to reach the settlement. But the gap between what Toadsmith experienced and what Molly, Gus, and Vance experienced in the same tunnels — and why three of the four people present returned while one did not — is a question the debrief does not answer because Toadsmith was not there to write the ending.

Waluigi holds the first assessment. He holds it with the particular stubbornness of someone who has been doing this long enough to know that most people who disappear from the historical record were not killed by dramatic violence but by the quieter process of deciding they needed to be somewhere nobody was looking. And he holds it because the debrief is too calm, too organized, too clearly the work of someone who expected to survive, for him to conclude otherwise.

He hopes.

## The Engineer — What Three Weeks Reveals That Forty Years Obscures


In the long view of history, the engineer is a shadow. A presence implied by gaps, by evidence chains that do not terminate at obvious sources, by the particular pattern of operations that required advance knowledge to design. Over eighty-five years, his tracks have been covered by time and institutional silence.

In the three-week timeline, he is almost visible.

The engineer visited Peach multiple times in the weeks before the assassination. Security footage shows a hooded figure entering through the hatch — the same hatch the assassin would use, the same passage Bowser's forces found when they arrived to discover her already dead. The engineer's gloves bore his initials. His bearing was distinctive enough for a guard to recognize it from a single prior encounter during castle repairs. He delivered a silver key whose function is not documented in any recovered record. He confirmed the blade's Guild sourcing in enough operational detail that Peach could write about it with precision.

He told her the enemy had been in the room with him for thirty years.

Three weeks after the assassination, his forces — or forces connected to him — arrived at Bowser's Castle by helicopter targeting the specific storage wing where the journal was held. This is not a coincidence of timing. This is an emergency retrieval operation conducted during the active construction phase of a cover-up, by a party who knew the journal existed because the journal documented his visits to the woman who had been murdered eight days after he last saw her.

He needed the journal because the journal proved he had helped a princess arrange her own death as an act of political warfare. That is not a comfortable piece of evidence to leave in an unsorted crate in a Koopa King's storage room.

Bowser's guard identified the silver bolt insignia. The E.M. emblem on the gloves. The bearing, the style, the particular operational fingerprint of someone who moves through other people's spaces with the confidence of a person accustomed to going where he is not invited.

Waluigi will not write the name here. Waluigi will note that the pattern is consistent, that the timeline matches, that the operations have a unified logic when viewed as the work of a single party, and that the reader is in possession of sufficient information to reach their own conclusions.

Waluigi will also note that the engineer's relationship to the conspiracy is complex. He helped build the plan. He helped Peach execute the plan. But the plan was, at its core, Peach's plan — a counter-conspiracy designed to expose the conspiracy from the inside, using her own death as the detonator. The engineer was her operational partner, not her controller. Whether he understood the full scope of what she was doing is unknown. Whether he wanted the journal suppressed because it implicated him in the conspiracy or because it implicated him in the counter-conspiracy — or both — is the question that Waluigi cannot yet resolve.

## What This


Incident Means — Wet Concrete and the First Crack

The Toadsmith Incident is significant not for what it resolved — it resolved nothing — but for what it established at a time when almost nothing was established.

Three weeks after the assassination, the Regency was still building its narrative. The cover-up was wet concrete, not hardened stone. The lie was new and still soft and still capable of being marked.

Toadsmith drove a crack into it before it set.

The crack did not break the structure. The concrete hardened around it. The Regency maintained its narrative for eighty-five years. Toadsworth Sr. consolidated power. The Guild suppressed the evidence. The official story became official history. The investigation was buried under the weight of institutional documentation that made the lie look like the product of legitimate process.

But the crack persisted. Cracks do not heal in concrete. They persist. They widen. Water gets in. Frost expands them. Roots find them.

The Loyalist movement found the crack. Archivist Inkwell found the guard rotation gap through it. Captain Toadette recovered Toadsworth Sr.'s journals through it. Mistveil extracted the Thornpaw revelation through it. Every subsequent discovery in eighty-five years of investigation passed through the opening that a mid-rank procedural investigator created in a Donut Plains market square three weeks after the assassination, in front of forty people, with a journal he was never supposed to find, in a crate that should have been catalogued and processed before he ever reached the storage room.

The journal has sat with a Donut Plains elder for eighty-five years. Whether it survived, whether it was moved or seized or hidden, whether it still exists as a physical document in 1040 BF, is unknown. The elder is almost certainly dead. The chain of custody is a thread Waluigi intends to follow.

But the information survived even if the journal did not. Because forty people heard it, and forty people are not a conspiracy, and the things that forty ordinary people hear in a market square do not disappear cleanly the way that documents can be burned and witnesses can be eliminated.

Waluigi returns to the central question that animates this investigation: what actually happened on Highsun 1, 955 BF?

The Chronicles say the Regency enabled it. Coronation Day says Peach chose it. The Toadsmith Incident says someone called the engineer helped coordinate it. The blade was Guild-sourced. The hatch was lover-sourced. The guard gap was Toadsworth-sourced. And the killer — the person in the third column of Peach's list, the person who held the blade — was someone the princess loved.

Waluigi does not have the name. Waluigi does not have the journal. Waluigi has fragments, contradictions, eighty-five years of accumulated speculation, and the unsigned intelligence note that arrived nine days after Captain Toadette seized Toad Town and the Regency's hold on its own narrative began cracking for the first time since the assassination.

Someone held this information for eighty-five years and chose now to release it. The structure protecting the secret is failing. The secrets are beginning to move.

Bloomia knows the name. She is findable, allegedly, in the place where roses grow in winter. Waluigi has theories about what that means. Waluigi intends to test them.
